newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt maintains economic pillars, lifts spending.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt maintains economic pillars, lifts spending.

text.p: The conservative National Party has doffed its hat to New Zealand First in most social policy areas, but kept the basic building blocks of its economic programme intact in the two parties' coalition manifesto.
In return, NZ First has traded away major elements of the nationalist policies which catapulted the party to almost 30 percent in opinion polls in early 1996.
A major surprise was the elevation of NZ First's charismatic Maori leader Winston Peters to the new post of Treasurer.

Peters, a minister in the National government before leaving to set up NZ First in 1993, was always expected to take the deputy's position but it appears he asked for the top finance job -- which includes the responsibility for writing the budget -- as a last-minute demand on National.

There is widespread speculation Peters and Prime Minister Jim Bolger, until recently bitter rivals, have a private understanding Bolger will step down during the three-year term to make way for Peters to lead the coalition.
At the general election on October 12, NZ First won 13 percent support -- enough to give it the balance of power.
After a protracted negotiation with both the conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party NZ First on Tuesday opted to join National.

The new government's policy programme, released on Wednesday, showed NZ First had traded away many of the nationalist policies which financial markets had feared, including strict curbs on overseas investment and immigration, a ban on all asset sales and the buyback of Forestry Corporation, sold for $2 billion in the run up to the October 12 election.
Its key policy of compulsory superannuation savings, designed to build up funds for the repurchase of assets by New Zealanders, will go to a binding referendum which is unlikely to succeed.
NZ First also dropped plans to reduce parliament from 120 to 100 MPs and limit the size of cabinet to 15.
The coalition manifesto lifts the size of the executive by two to 20 ministers inside cabinet and six outside. Of NZ First's 17 MPs, nine will initially be in the executive, rising to 11 in 1998.
Health and education combined account for the bulk of the $5 billion extra spending over three years.
A surtax on pensions, which cost National dearly among older voters, has been scrapped and NZ First's employment policy has been accepted unchanged.

In health, in particular, the previous National government's blueprint has been radically revamped. Hospitals have been freed of the profit motive and the four regional health authorities, which purchased services from the hospitals, have been conflated into one funding body.

There is also significant extra spending on areas of concern to Maori, who are over-represented in all statistics of social and economic deprivation in New Zealand. NZ First won all five seats reserved for Maori.

The previous government's $1 billion cap on the settlement of all historical Maori land and fishing grievances is scrapped. But the key elements of National's economic policies are virtually unchanged.

The employer-friendly industrial relations law, the Employment Contracts Act, will be amended only at the margins, while the expansion of the central bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent was well-signalled and would have been part of a Labour-New Zealand First agreement too.

The coalition will continue National's programme to reduce debt and taxes, although more slowly, and plans substantial, though lower, surpluses until the turn of the century. However a $1.1 billion tax cut planned for 1997 has been deferred to make way for the extra social spending.

The manifesto dilutes NZ First's blanket ban on asset sales to a list including power generators Electricorp and Contact Energy, grid operator Trans Power, NZ Post, TV1 and Radio New Zealand and makes no mention of the repurchase of Forestcorp.

The limit of 24.9 percent NZ First wanted on foreign ownership of key strategic assets has been dropped. Power and gas utilities, airports and ports owned by local bodies or consumer trusts must gain approval of ratepayers or consumers for sales to foreigners of more than 24.9 percent.
Restrictions on the sale of farm land will be tightened to strengthen "national interest" criteria.

The impression left by the programme is that NZ First is happy to continue its repositioning as a centre-right party, while National has recognised major social policy concessions will be needed to retain power under the new proportional representation system. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
